title: Comments & the Zen of Python
objective: Write useful comments and understand Python's preference for simple, readable code.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A comment starts with # and everything after it on that line is ignored by Python. Comments exist for the people reading the code, not the interpreter.

The most useful comments explain why a piece of code exists or what nonobvious decision it makes — not what a line does, since well-named variables and functions usually make that clear on their own. A comment repeating the code in English adds noise instead of value.

Python's design carries a well-known philosophy: code that is easy to read is more valuable than code that is merely clever. Favoring a straightforward solution over a compressed, tricky one tends to save far more time later, when someone (often you) has to come back and understand it again.
explanation.rule: Write a comment when the why isn't obvious from the code itself — skip it when the code already speaks for itself.

examples.title: A Comment That Earns Its Place
examples.code:
# Discount applied after midnight promo; remove after the event ends
price = 40 * 0.8
print(price)
examples.note: The comment explains a reason that isn't visible in the math itself.

checks.question: Which comment is more useful to a future reader?
options:
# retry limit; increase if the flaky network check keeps failing
count = count + 1

# this is a variable
count = count + 1

feedback.correct: Correct — it explains a reason that isn't visible in the code itself.
feedback.incorrect: The best comments explain why, not what — the code already shows what happens.

assignment.title: Documented Discount
assignment.brief: Write apply_discount() with at least one comment explaining why, that prints exactly: 32.0
requirements: Include at least one comment line starting with #.
Print exactly: 32.0 (the result of 40 multiplied by 0.8).
assignment.starterCode:
def apply_discount():
    # Add a comment explaining the discount, then print the result.
    pass

apply_discount()
assignment.solutionCode:
def apply_discount():
    # 20% off during the anniversary sale
    price = 40 * 0.8
    print(price)

apply_discount()
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    apply_discount()
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: 40 * 0.8 gives a float result because one of the values has a decimal point.
Your comment should explain why the discount exists, not just restate the math.
Print the calculated price, not a typed-out 32.0.
A comment line starts with #, anywhere in the function.
